lesson.title: Build a Python Calculator
lesson.overview: We'll build a calculator that runs in the terminal. First an add function you can test right away, then subtract, multiply and divide, with a guard so dividing by zero can't crash it. Then the program asks for two numbers and an operator, picks the right function and prints the result.

primer.title: Functions are reusable recipes
primer.body: A function is a named block of code. You give it inputs, like a and b, it does the work, and return hands the result back so you can use it.
primer.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

primer.title: Running a .py file
primer.body: Python reads your file from top to bottom and runs each line. Typing python3 calculator.py in the terminal runs it and shows anything it prints.

primer.title: Reading what the user types
primer.body: input() pauses the program until you type something and press Enter. It always gives back text, so float() turns that text into a number you can do maths with.

primer.title: Choosing with if, elif, else
primer.body: if runs its indented lines only when its condition is true. elif tries the next condition, and else catches everything that matched nothing above.

steps.title: Write an add function
steps.what: An add function that adds two numbers
steps.why: Every calculator operation will be a small function like this one, so you can test each piece on its own.
steps.action: In calculator.py, type the add function and its test line below the comment
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, type the add function and the print line below the comment.

precision_checks.label: The test line is in calculator.py

targets.match: # Step 1: Start building your calculator here
targets.caption: In calculator.py, type the add function and its test line below the comment

hints: Click at the end of the comment line, press Enter, and type the def line.
The return line sits inside add, so indent it by four spaces.
Leave a blank line, type print(add(2, 3)) at the left edge, then save with Cmd+S.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the colon at the end of def add(a, b):.
Not indenting return a + b, which gives an IndentationError.
Indenting the print line, which puts it inside add where it never runs.
Forgetting to save, so the terminal runs the old, empty file.

steps.title: Run your calculator
steps.what: Run your calculator and see it print 5
steps.why: Running the file makes Python follow your code line by line, so you can see that add(2, 3) really gives 5.
steps.action: Run python3 calculator.py in the VS Code terminal
steps.instructions: In the terminal, run python3 calculator.py and check that it prints 5.

precision_checks.label: The test line is in calculator.py

hints: Open the terminal with Ctrl+` if it isn't showing.
Type python3 calculator.py exactly and press Enter.
You should see 5 on its own line. An error means a typo in add or in the print line.
common_mistakes: Typing python instead of python3: this Mac only has python3.
Running before saving, so nothing prints.
Running from another folder, which gives No such file or directory.

steps.title: Add three more operations
steps.why: With all four operations as functions, the calculator can call whichever one the user asks for.
steps.action: In calculator.py, type subtract, multiply and divide above the print line
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, type the three functions below, above the print line.

targets.caption: In calculator.py, type subtract, multiply and divide above the print line

hints: Put the cursor at the start of the print line and press Enter to make room above it.
Each function is a def line plus an indented return line, just like add.
subtract uses a - b, multiply uses a * b, and divide uses a / b.
common_mistakes: Typing b - a or b / a: keep a on the left.
Missing the colon after (a, b) or the indent under def.
Adding a zero check to divide now: that comes in the next step.

steps.title: Guard against dividing by zero
steps.why: Dividing by zero crashes Python, so divide() stops early with a clear error message instead.
steps.action: In calculator.py, add the zero check inside divide(), under its def line
steps.instructions: Inside divide(), type the two lines below between its def line and its return line.
steps.code:
if b == 0:
    raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero")

checks.label: The zero error message is typed

precision_checks.label: The zero check is in calculator.py
The error message is in calculator.py

targets.caption: In calculator.py, add the zero check inside divide(), under its def line

hints: Click at the end of the def divide(a, b): line and press Enter; VS Code indents for you.
Type if b == 0: and press Enter; the raise line goes one level deeper.
Use two equals signs: == compares, = assigns.
common_mistakes: Writing if b = 0: with one equals sign, a SyntaxError.
Putting the check below return a / b, where it never runs.
Forgetting the colon after if b == 0.
Indenting raise at the same level as if, so it always runs.

steps.title: Read the user's input
steps.what: A main() function that asks for two numbers and an operator
steps.why: input() lets the person at the keyboard choose the numbers, and float() turns their text into numbers you can calculate with.
steps.action: In calculator.py, replace print(add(2, 3)) with the main() function below
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, delete the print(add(2, 3)) line and type main() in its place.
steps.code:
def main():
    first = float(input("First number: "))
    op = input("Operator (+, -, *, /): ")
    second = float(input("Second number: "))

targets.caption: In calculator.py, replace print(add(2, 3)) with the main() function below

hints: Select the whole print(add(2, 3)) line and type over it.
The three lines inside main() are indented by four spaces.
input() always returns text; float() turns it into a number. The operator stays text.
common_mistakes: Leaving print(add(2, 3)) in the file, so 5 prints every time.
Forgetting the parentheses or the colon in def main():.
Wrapping the operator in float(), which fails on +.
Missing a closing parenthesis in float(input(...)), a SyntaxError.

steps.title: Pick the operation
steps.what: An if/elif chain that picks the right operation
steps.why: The operator the user typed decides which of your four functions runs, and the answer is printed as Result.
steps.action: Inside main(), type the if/elif lines under the second number line
steps.instructions: Inside main(), type the lines below under the line that reads the second number, indented four spaces.

precision_checks.label: The divide branch is in calculator.py
The result line is in calculator.py

targets.caption: Inside main(), type the if/elif lines under the second number line

hints: Each if, elif and else line ends with a colon, and the line under it is indented four more spaces.
Compare op with a string in quotes, like op == "+".
The last print line lines up with if, not with result.
common_mistakes: Writing op == + without quotes, a SyntaxError.
Using = instead of == in a comparison.
Indenting the Result print under else, so it never prints a result.

steps.title: Call main() at the bottom
steps.what: A line that starts main() when you run the file
steps.why: Python runs main() only when you start calculator.py yourself, not when another file imports it.
steps.action: At the very bottom of calculator.py, type the main guard, not indented
steps.instructions: At the very bottom of calculator.py, type the two lines below, with if at the left edge.

precision_checks.label: The main guard is in calculator.py
main() is called under the guard

targets.caption: At the very bottom of calculator.py, type the main guard, not indented

hints: Click at the end of the last line, press Enter, then Backspace until the cursor is at the left edge.
__name__ and "__main__" each have two underscores on both sides.
main() goes on the next line, indented four spaces.
common_mistakes: Indenting the if line, which puts it inside main() where it never runs.
Writing "main" without the underscores.
Leaving main() unindented, so it runs outside the guard.

steps.title: Try your calculator
steps.what: Run your calculator and divide 8 by 2
steps.why: A real run shows every piece working together: your input, the chosen operation and the printed result.
steps.action: Run python3 calculator.py in the VS Code terminal, then enter 8, / and 2
steps.instructions: In the terminal, run python3 calculator.py, then type 8, / and 2, pressing Enter after each.

precision_checks.label: The main guard is in calculator.py

hints: Run python3 calculator.py; it waits for you at First number:.
Type 8 and Enter, then / and Enter, then 2 and Enter.
Seeing 4.0 rather than 4 is right: float() makes the numbers decimals.
common_mistakes: Typing all three answers on one line instead of pressing Enter after each.
Typing divide instead of the / symbol, which prints Unknown operator.
Running before saving, so the old file runs and nothing is asked.
